interviewQuestions.question: Your app breaks when a user's node restarts — why, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd diagnose it as a statelessness violation first: if restarting one node logs users out or loses their cart, their session data was almost certainly living in that node's local memory, possibly reinforced by sticky sessions pinning them there in the first place.

The fix is moving session state out of the app process entirely, into something every node can reach — Redis is the standard choice — so any server can pick up any request and still know who the user is. I'd walk through the migration concretely: read/write session data through a Redis client instead of an in-memory map, then I can safely remove the sticky-session requirement, since any node now serves any request correctly.

I'd close by noting stickiness itself isn't inherently bad — it's using it as your *only* session storage that's the actual bug.

**Testing:** whether you trace the symptom (node restart breaks users) back to the real root cause (state living on one machine) instead of treating stickiness as the fix.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing and fixing node-restart breakage

interviewQuestions.question: What's the trade-off with using sticky sessions?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as convenience now for reliability later. Sticky sessions let an app work without any session-store infrastructure, which is genuinely appealing for a quick fix or an MVP.

The cost shows up in exactly the moments you need the system most: uneven load if pinned clients happen to be heavy users, a spike of broken sessions the instant a pinned server dies or gets redeployed, and new servers not helping already-pinned clients at all. So it isn't that stickiness is simply 'bad' — it's that it silently removes the load balancer's ability to route around failure for the clients who are pinned.

I'd conclude that stickiness is fine as a *performance* optimization on top of externalized state, but risky as your only mechanism for keeping users logged in.

**Testing:** whether you can name the concrete failure modes, not just say 'stickiness is an anti-pattern.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The real cost of session affinity

interviewQuestions.question: When, if ever, would you choose sticky sessions on purpose?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd say it's justified when the data genuinely can't move cheaply, not as a shortcut around building a session store. A concrete example: a WebSocket connection is inherently pinned to whichever server accepted it — there's no meaningful way to 'externalize' an open socket — so routing later messages on that same connection back to the same node isn't a workaround, it's just how the protocol works.

Another case: a game server or real-time system holding large, frequently-updated in-memory state per session, where a round trip to an external store on every update would blow the latency budget the feature needs to work at all.

I'd draw the line clearly: stickiness for data that structurally must live on one machine is a reasonable trade-off; stickiness to avoid building Redis-backed sessions for an ordinary web app is the anti-pattern.

**Testing:** whether you can distinguish a legitimate architectural reason for affinity from using it as a substitute for real state management.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Legitimate uses of sticky sessions
